Messages.Author: Johan Lundstrom
Messages.Body:
"Players must play each game toward the goal stated in the rulebook of
gaining the most victory points in the current game."

How strictly should this be interpreted? As written, it would seem to
make deal-breaking mandatory in some situations. For instance:

I and my predator both play rush decks. I've made a deal with my
predator to split the table 3-2, and I've bashed my way through three
preys, co I'm currently at 3 VP's, and according to the deal, I should
fold now. However, I'm in pretty good shape and I'd have a good chance
to defeat the guy I made the deal with and sweep. It seems the rule as
written would forbid me to honour the agreement and let him get the 2
last VP's - neither personal honour (yeah, right) or reputation (more
likely) could possibly be said to be an in-game consideration.

Is this a correct interpretation of the rule? Are players in
tournaments forbidden to honour their deals if it can be demonstrated
that they have nothing to benefit (in-game) from keeping them?

-----------------------------------------------------------
Johan Lundstrom <jo...@algonet.se>

This, to me, is actually the interesting question. Having made a deal to
split victory points and having collected the victory points that one player
(no matter whether the "3" player or the "2" player or whatever points the
player given the initial benefit was assigned to receive), that player is
pretty much in the driver's seat as the game is ending. So he could probably
break the deal at that point and keep the last 2 (or 3 or whatever) victory
points to himself. I think the kind of controversial statement LSJ is making
is that it's not then an "out-of-game consideration" to be honorable and keep
a deal. I think some people have a very arguable case that the only possible
reason to keep a deal at this point is one's reputation for keeping deals, which
seems clearly an out-of-game consideration by itself. Anything more seems a
completely philosophical argument failing the ability to time-travel or psychically
communicate backwards in time.

Of course, if this one of those, "because-the-design-team-said-so" type of
deals, I wouldn't waste my time worrying about it. But I think some people
here view this point as a way to discourage such deals which many dislike: if
you can prevent the player in control of the board from keeping his half of the
deal at the end of the game and handing those last 2 VPs to his deal-partner by
invoking the "no out-of-game-consideration" rule, then such victory point
splitting deals would be a lot harder for players to work. Just an observation.
I wanted to put my foot into what I think is the heart of the matter because I
hadn't seen it discussed elsewhere. (My apologies if it was and I just missed
it.) I'd like to hear LSJ's comments on this in particular.

Fred

Yes, I suppose it would have that implication. I'm not totally sure that would be
a bad thing in and of itself. I've never seen these kinds of hard-and-fast deals
to do anything for the fun of the game. I'd rather people stick to deals that were
very short term, myself.

Still, I can see where this would get to be a real problem for judges, as certain
types of mid-term deals would land in a gray area of enforceability. If four players
are on the board and two of them make a deal which will help one immediately oust
one of the player in return for some future consideration, it might be hard to judge
whether it breaks the out-of-game consideration rule to keep the other end of the
deal. Now there's three players and the one getting the initial benefit may have the
upper hand but it's a matter of judgment whether he'd have a better chance to win
the game if his deal-partner where to punish him for not keeping their deal. I can
see where it might be better not ever have judges trying to figure that out.

Fred

This won't wash. Try games like Reiner Knizia's Lord of the Rings,
the MB Buffy game, Avalon Hill's Republic of Rome and Diplomacy. And
poker. Or Hofstadter's Mediocrity - a game in which the player with
a middling number of points is the winner.

Issues of this sort were much discussed when I played a lot of
Diplomacy. In that game, victory is secured by gaining a majority of
supply centres, just as victory in VTES is obtained by gaining a
majority of victory points. This leads to the "obvious" idea that the
player with the second-most number of supply centres has come second
and so on. A lot of players, including the designer, repudiated this
idea and took the view that there was a winner or winner(s) and
everyone else had lost. For rating purposes, some even proposed that
the player with the second-most number of supply centres should suffer
the greatest penalty because he was in the best position to stop the
winner and had failed to do so.

Contrariwise, in poker, the game objective is to maximise your money.
There is no formal winner and someone who wins a small amount may be
happier with the result than someone who wins a large amount - it's
just a matter of expectations.

If there is no formal definition of places then it's often the
metagame which determines what value players place upon different
losing outcomes. In the case of poker the usual metagame is money.
In the case of Diplomacy the usual metagame was ratings. The usual
metagame for VTES is the tournament - no-one seems to care much about
their rating. By the current rules, 2 VP is worth quite a bit in a
qualifying round. Its value in the final depends upon the prizes and
kudos.

The VEKN is trying to outlaw some metagame considerations but not
others - revenge for a broken deal is forbidden but keeping a bad deal
for the sake of your reputation is ok. Rushing a player because he's
known to be strong is forbidden but declining to rush a player who's
weak is ok (I suppose). I'm not sure I have a good solution but there
is a real problem here. Establishing what players are supposed to be
trying to do is just the start.

Andrew

The lack of a formal definition of places still does not prevent players from
inventing these concepts within their playgroups, and seems to be fairly common,
IME, and from most reports. Believe it or not, in many local playgroups, a less
strict (read: wrong) interpretation of the rules was held, and the last person
standing was usually seen as the winner, whether or not he actually ousted
anyone aside from the last remaining person. I would like to believe (though
obviously have no evidence) that more people see the world (and games) as a
ordinal ranking, rather than a strictly binary win-loss situation. And I have
seen ample evidence of the anecdote of consoling oneself with the status of
"second place."

All things aside, second place (and so on) are useful concepts in terms of the
game (not just the tournament) as they will frequently allow players to gauge
how well their decks performed in comparison with other players. If (as
happened last night in my playgroup), my deck had not taken 4 VPs at a 6 player
table, and instead had taken 2VPs (scored by the other remaining player in the
endgame), I might have reconsidered my play or my deck strategy, realizing that
something may have been amiss, though not as much off as the other 4 players who
failed to score a VP. My final opponent's deck demonstrably scored better than
all of the other players, but resulted in a loss, true. He can, however,
justifiably state that he did not lose by as much (in terms of VPs) as any of
the other players...practically a description of the concept of second place.

> metagame for VTES is the tournament - no-one seems to care much about
> their rating. By the current rules, 2 VP is worth quite a bit in a

You do have a point here that there is a problem. I agree.

To go point by point:

a) revenge for a broken deal is forbidden

Revenge for a broken deal in a separate game is forbidden.

b) but keeping a bad deal for the sake of your reputation is ok.

Because you made that deal within this game. As LSJ has pointed out if this
were *not* allowed, deals would never be made, and it would definitely require
additional "play-policing" on the part of the judges...neither of which is a
desirable situation.

c) Rushing a player because he's known to be strong is forbidden

Rushing a player because you know that he plays well before the game has
unfolded itself *and* you cannot indicate any other reason for doing so is
forbidden.

d) but declining to rush a player who's weak is ok (I suppose).

I assume you mean "prey" in place of "player" in the above. There are many
situations where you wouldn't want to rush a weak prey. Perhaps he can whittle
down his prey for you, while you keep him close to death's door. Perhaps you're
happy just slowly bleeding away his pool instead of rushing his minions (this is
sometimes the most effective tactic for a rush deck).

Yes, there is a problem, and it's attempting to be addressed by the new rules.
Although I'm not sure that the table victory is the best direction to go for
tournaments, it's a new idea, and a good one. Thank you.

As with any new rules, it will take some time to see if they are effective at
producing the desired results...let's give it a chance before attempting to
render a final verdict.

I'd prefer that solemn and binding deals were not made as they spoil
the game for the following reasons:

1. If you have absolute trust in another player then powerful deals
can be made, e.g. giving all your minions with Succubus Club. These
swing the game too much.

2. You get too much bad feeling and arguments when they are broken or
the terms are disputed, e.g. recent examples in both London and LA.

3. The habitual use of these deals discriminates against new players
and outsiders. They are de facto collusion. You can see this in the
way that players from the same city are driven to form coalitions.
This appears to be a standard feature of US events.

4. They often subvert the basic objective of the game which is
supposed to be ousting your prey. For a predator to leave his prey
alone for an extended period is not right.

At the Watford pre-release, there was a deal of this kind. The
Giovanni player was trying to steal a mummy from his predator, the Set
player. His prey, the Assamite, could interfere with this but
suggested that he would not if the Giovanni agreed not to bleed him
until the Set player had been ousted. I was Ravnos, the prey of the
Assamite and didn't like the sound of this but didn't know enough of
the details to argue against it. I probed a little though and it
became clear that the Giovanni player and Assamite were known to each
other, expected to play again and would under no circumstances break
this deal. This had the effect of raising an impenetrable wall
between the Giovanni and Assamite player and the latter swept the
table in consequence.

The lesson is clear to me. It's only worth playing in an event if it
is packed with your friends and known associates. Yuck.

It doesn't have to be this way. Shadowfist games are usually 4-player
but the tournaments for this game are remarkably free of this kind of
rigid, long-term deal-making and "us against them". This probably
arises because a victory is indivisible and there is no way for allies
to share the spoils. Helping another player to win in a direct way
would normally be regarded as prima facie evidence of collusion and so
struck down. This then sets the tone for the rest of the game and
alliances tend to be fleeting affairs - just temporary coalitions of
the weak against the strong. The games are basically "every man for
himself" and this seems to work better.

>d) but declining to rush a player who's weak is ok (I suppose).
>
>I assume you mean "prey" in place of "player" in the above.

No, it might be any player that you would have good reason to rush
otherwise, e.g. your predator or grand-predator. It's just the
converse of the case which is forbidden.

Andrew

Alright. I think it should be emphasized just how much is required for
a game to be 'provably lost':

* Your losing should not depend on predicted actions by anyone, only
by effects or actions currently in place (X is bleeding you, there's
an Anarch Revolt in play, and so on, *not* 'He could bleed me to death
if he wanted to').
* No one else at the table could, even theory, save you. This includes
a (theoretical) Life Boon, Eagle's Sight or anything else.
* Even card cycling with a perfect draw by you, or anyone else, could
save you even in theory.
* If anyone can construe a hypothetical solution, no matter how
unlikely, that lets you get off the hook, you're not allowed to play
as though you had lost.

(LSJ, do you agree on these?)

This situation is highly, no, *extremely* unlikely to occur. I even
think there are situations where it couldn't possibly occur. For
instance, you would never be allowed to transfer out, if the
conditions could never apply in the transfer phase (which, as far as I
can see, they can't).
